Project Goals/Objectives Our objective is to overcome the limitations in conventional drying and water removal processes in pulp and paper and other biomaterials manufacturing by integrating modern process intensified technologies. Integration of cross-cutting, electrically-powered technologies thus reducing the thermal budget of the drying process drying represents a significant opportunity and is a priority. The overall project stretch goal was to increase the drying rate and production/throughput rate by 30% (minimum 20%) and decrease the drying energy consumption by 30% (minimum 20%) in pulp and paper manufacturing. In addition, our goal was to reduce the carbon intensity by 50% (minimum 25%) and reduce the operating costs including energy costs by 30% (minimum 20%). This technology could have potential cross-cutting application across multiple industries including pulp and paper, biomaterials, food, and other process industries. One of the main objectives of this study was to experimentally determine the drying characteristics of paper under commercial conditions of alternating conductive and convective drying with instantaneous monitoring and acquisition of all drying parameters (air, sample, and hot-plate temperatures, flow rate, humidity, contact pressure, absolute pressure) at very high resolutions and accuracies. This will help establish the baseline drying characteristics. Integration of RF and US energies would then enable us to determine their drying performance and compare with conventional drying processes. Results and Discussion The first part of the work was to demonstrate the proof-of-concept of the proposed technology of using RF and US in conjunction with conventional drying. This was accomplished by collaborators using small pieces of paper 1”-2” in size and evaluation of convective and conductive drying and application of RF and US energies by our DOE national laboratory partner. These experiments demonstrated that the integration of these technologies increased the 10 DE-EE0009395 drying rate by a minimum of 10% compared to baseline conventional drying and 10% decrease in energy consumption. The experimental approach also provided some key insights in the development of the larger scale, more detailed experimental evaluation. Experimental Setup Based on a thorough review of the literature, proof-of-concept work, discussions with project collaborators and industry partners, the design, measurement techniques and process conditions for the large scale (8” x 8” paper sample size) experimental drying setup were developed. A complex and challenging design involving alternating contact conduction and convection, more closely simulating the commercial paper machine drying process, and appropriate integration of auxiliary energy (RF and US), was selected for the final experimental setup design.
